questions.title: Why is prior possession of the same firearm considered 'intrinsic evidence' rather than Rule 404(b) propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Cutbank and the court holds that D.F.'s testimony about seeing Cutbank with the sawed-off rifle before the incident is 'intrinsic evidence' and not subject to Rule 404(b). But isn't the whole point of 404(b) to prevent the jury from convicting someone because they're a 'bad person' who has done bad things before? If the defendant possessed the same gun before, that seems like it would invite the jury to think 'he's the type of person who walks around with sawed-off rifles.' How does the 'same weapon' factor make this intrinsic rather than extrinsic propensity evidence? And what's the practical boundary between intrinsic and 404(b) evidence in possession cases?

questions.title: Does the Confrontation Clause require a limiting instruction when officers testify about a victim's out-of-court statements before the victim testifies?
questions.question_body: Cutbank requested a limiting instruction to prevent the jury from considering D.F.'s statements to police as substantive evidence until she testified. The court denied this, saying the statements were admitted for context and that D.F. eventually testified, satisfying the Confrontation Clause. But I'm confused about the timing issue—if officers testify about what D.F. told them before D.F. takes the stand, hasn't the jury already heard hearsay statements that could be used substantively? Does the Confrontation Clause only care about whether the declarant testifies at some point, or does the sequence matter? And when should a limiting instruction be required?

questions.title: How does Rule 403 apply when a witness's testimony about personal trauma (sister killed by gun) is elicited to explain prior inconsistent statements?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination about her prior inconsistent statements, D.F. mentioned that her sister was killed by a gun, which seems highly prejudicial in a firearms case. The court denied Cutbank's motion to strike, saying this 'responded to cross-examination regarding inconsistent prior statements.' I understand that evidence responding to cross-examination can be relevant, but the probative value of why she made inconsistent statements seems minimal compared to the prejudice of having the jury hear about gun-related death. How do courts actually apply the Rule 403 balancing test in situations like this? What threshold of prejudice is required?

questions.title: What foundation is required to admit a police report for impeachment by prior inconsistent statement when the witness didn't author the report?
questions.question_body: The court sustained the government's objection to defense counsel reading portions of a police report to impeach C.F., noting the report was not authored by C.F. and lacked proper foundation. But I thought the rule against extrinsic evidence for collateral matters (Rule 608(b)) was the main limit on impeachment by prior inconsistent statement. If C.F. gave a statement to police that was reduced to writing by an officer, can the defense use that report at all? Does C.F. need to authenticate that the report accurately reflects what she said, or does the officer need to testify? What's the proper way to get a prior inconsistent statement from a police interview before the jury?

questions.title: What standard governs whether a firearm was possessed 'in connection with' another felony for USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement purposes?
questions.question_body: The court applied a four-level enhancement under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) because Cutbank possessed the firearm 'in connection with another felony offense.' The opinion notes that the PSR established he committed domestic abuse, kidnapping, and assault while possessing the gun. But how close must the connection be between the firearm possession and the other felony? If someone possesses a firearm and also commits a felony during the same time period but the gun wasn't used in the felony, does that still count? The commentary says 'regardless of whether a criminal charge was brought, or a conviction obtained'—does that mean the sentencing judge can find facts supporting the 'other felony' even if no charge was filed? What's the legal standard for 'in connection with'?

questions.title: How do ACCA enhancements interact with USSG § 2K2.1 sentencing enhancements when both would apply?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that Cutbank's ACCA status would have produced a total offense level of 34, but the § 2K2.1 calculations resulted in level 35, and 'the greater offense level applies' under USSG § 4B1.4(b). I'm struggling to understand how these two frameworks interact. Does ACCA establish a floor, a ceiling, or something else entirely? And if the court is required to apply the greater offense level, does that effectively mean the ACCA guidelines are subordinate to the regular firearms guidelines when the latter produce a higher level? What's the policy rationale for this hierarchy?

questions.title: Does the presumption of reasonableness for within-guidelines sentences conflict with § 3553(a)'s requirement that sentences be 'not greater than necessary'?
questions.question_body: Cutbank argued that the four-level enhancement resulted in a sentence that 'conflicts with the core principle of 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)' that a sentence be 'sufficient, but not greater than necessary.' The court applied a presumption of reasonableness to the within-guidelines sentence and affirmed. But if the guidelines themselves can produce sentences that are 'greater than necessary,' how does presuming those sentences are reasonable square with the statutory mandate? Does the presumption effectively shift the burden to the defendant to prove the sentence is excessive, and is that consistent with the statutory text? I'm confused about the relationship between appellate presumption and the district court's obligation to impose a sentence that is 'not greater than necessary.'
